| [THEORY-170](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-170.md) v2 | Languages differ in what their grammar obliges a speaker to convey rather than in what they can convey, so interlingual translation must add some information and leave some unexpressed, and repeated translation can erode a message | Jakobson (1959), [LIT-786](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-786.md), after Boas: every cognitive content can be expressed in any language, but each grammar obliges its speakers to answer certain questions (aspect, number, gender, tense, definiteness). Translating between grammars that ask different questions forces the translator to supply answers the source did not give and to leave unexpressed answers it did, and a chain of translations of an isolated sentence can lose its content, less so the richer the context. Argued from examples, not tested; it concerns cognitive content, not pragmatic force. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-226](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-226.md) | LLM revisions of an essay move it further in sentence-embedding space than its author's own revision does, and in a direction shared across essays, models and prompts | Abdulhai et al. Three LLMs revising 86 ArgRewrite-v2 drafts under five prompts moved them further than the students' own 2021 revisions did, and in one common direction, under two embeddings. | [THEORY-1120](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1120.md) v2 | On 416 translations into English by four LLMs of 104 culturally loaded utterances in Hindi, Punjabi, Tamil and Malayalam, each scored for pragmatic adequacy by one native rater per language, the reference-based COMET metric correlates with the ratings at Pearson r = 0.813 and Spearman ρ = 0.860, against r 0.80 and ρ 0.79 for XCOMET and r 0.73 and ρ 0.79 for MetricX, with no test of the differences; four outputs picked after the fact that invert or misplace the source's meaning get COMET scores of 0.65–0.86 against the rater's 1 or 2 | Singh et al. On 416 outputs (104 items × 4 models), wmt22 COMET correlates with 1–5 pragmatic-adequacy scores at Pearson 0.813, Spearman 0.860; XCOMET ρ 0.792, MetricX ρ 0.788 (Table 3). Four hand-picked outputs scored 0.65–0.86 by COMET and 1–2 by the rater. Each language had one rater, so there is no reliability against which to read 0.81, and the claim that metrics fail "especially for implicature and deixis" rests on per-phenomenon differences of 0.1 or less. | Active |
| [THEORY-1134](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1134.md) v2 | A translation metric that predicts a sentence score and token-level error spans from one shared encoder reaches segment-level agreement with expert MQM annotation of Kendall τ about 0.4 and span F1 under 0.33, the best among open metrics and GPT-4 prompting at the time, while the score computed from its own spans correlates with its regression scores at Pearson 0.73 to 0.82, and at 0.90 to 0.92 with its final score, which includes the span score by construction | Guerreiro, Rei, van Stigt, Coheur, Colombo and Martins (TACL 2024), [LIT-1816](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1816.md), Tables 2, 4 and 5, read in [NOTE-1341](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1341.md). | [THEORY-1142](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1142.md) | A translation between two logics presented as institutions is correct, in the Satisfaction Condition's sense, when a translated sentence holds in a model exactly when the original holds in the model's translation; given the model translation this fixes the sentence translation up to semantic equivalence, and when every model of the target is reached it preserves and reflects entailment, so one logic's prover can decide the other's; but the condition alone admits collapsing translations and is relative to a model translation it does not supply | Goguen and Burstall (1992), [LIT-1661](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1661.md), read in [NOTE-1348](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1348.md) from the published JACM article: Definition 32 (p. 125), Proposition 33 and Proposition 35 (p. 126), Theorem 39 (pp. 127–129). Active: proved, and checked on toy morphisms between propositional institutions. The collapsing morphism and the atom-negating morphism are my constructions, not the paper's. | [THEORY-1143](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1143.md) | When one domain carries more information than the other, a translation trained only to make the round trip close cannot meet that requirement through a correspondence in the intermediate's visible code, so the round trip closes through a channel the intermediate's audience does not read; agreement of the round trip with its source therefore says nothing about whether the intermediate renders the source's content for that audience | Chu, Zhmoginov and Sandler (2017), [LIT-1800](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1800.md), §2 and §5, read in [NOTE-1346](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1346.md). The authors argue it from the many photographs a single map stands for, and support it with [THEORY-1127](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1127.md)'s evidence on one model; they propose, and do not run, the test of adding capacity to the smaller domain. Proposed. It is the converse of the record's collapse case for [CLAIM-496](../../../record/claims.d/CLAIM-496.md): there routes agree because nothing travels, here because everything does, out of sight. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1145](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1145.md) | Unsupervised alignment of two monolingual word-embedding spaces recovers translations only where the spaces are close to isometric, and the distance from isometry depends on the corpora and the embedding algorithm as well as on the languages: adversarial alignment fails for English with Estonian or Finnish, across corpus domains, and between skip-gram and CBOW spaces of the same language pair, GW alignment is weakest on the same Finnish pair, and a spectral dissimilarity of small nearest-neighbour graphs tracks success | Søgaard, Ruder and Vulić (2018), [LIT-1819](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1819.md), read in [NOTE-1337](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1337.md), with the GW results of Alvarez-Melis and Jaakkola (2018), [LIT-1818](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1818.md), read in [NOTE-1336](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1336.md).
